subject: physics
title: Wien's Law and Stefan-Boltzmann
welcome_lead: Use a star's colour and luminosity to read its temperature with Wien and Stefan.
meta_desc: A-Level Astrophysics adventure on Wien's displacement law and Stefan-Boltzmann radiation.
final_note: Colour gives T, area + T gives luminosity — astrophysics in two equations.

concepts.def: The distance light travels in one year (~9.5×10¹⁵ m).
v = 2πr ÷ T for a body in a circular orbit.
A stable star fusing hydrogen to helium, gravity balanced by radiation pressure.
Late stages of a low-mass star's life.
The explosive death of a massive star, leaving a neutron star or black hole.

walkthroughs.body_html: λ_max × T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. A blue star (small λ_max) is hot; a red star is cool. The Sun peaks near 500 nm at about 5800 K.
Luminosity scales with surface area and the fourth power of temperature. Hotter, bigger stars are spectacularly brighter than cooler small ones.
From spectrum get T (Wien). From measured L (using flux + distance) compute area A = L / (σ T⁴), and hence radius R = √(A/4π).

options: λ_max × T = constant
λ_max / T = constant
λ_max + T = constant
T / λ_max² = constant

Why do brighter-looking stars not necessarily have higher luminosity?
options: Apparent brightness depends only on the star's temperature.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance — a closer dim star can look brighter than a distant luminous one.
Brighter-looking stars are always intrinsically more luminous.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
